script.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.

terra.problem: The explanation places David lying down beside the waters. The verse says the LORD makes him lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters.
The explanation sounds like a dictionary entry. Phrases such as 'putting something to the proof' and 'renewal rather than examination' are stiff for Papa.
Explaining what 'His' points to and then cataloging the parts of the verse sounds mechanical rather than like Papa.
The instruction to separate 'the place in the picture' from 'the reason in the sentence' is clinical and generic.
The verse says David's head is anointed with oil, not his hair.
The closing contrast between 'a particular pair' and 'a general list of desirable things' sounds like generic instructional copy, not Papa.

explanations.explanation: David, the writer of this psalm, says he will lack nothing with the LORD as his shepherd (Psalm 23:1). Here, want means being without what he needs. Friend, this is confidence in his shepherd's care, not a list of things he hopes to collect.

Earn is about working to receive something, baker. David is talking about not lacking what he needs because the LORD is his shepherd (Psalm 23:1). This line expresses trust in that care, not a promise that David will never work.

Losing something and lacking what you need are different things. David says he will not want, meaning he will not lack what he needs with the LORD as his shepherd (Psalm 23:1). He isn't saying that nothing will ever go missing.

The lying down, green pastures, and quiet waters give this picture its restful feel (Psalm 23:2). Nothing in that scene suggests a frantic scramble. I can turn searching for my apron into a frantic scramble while I'm WEARING it.

Hustle has you hurrying to get somewhere or finish something. Here, the LORD makes David lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters (Psalm 23:2). Friend, let the lying down slow the picture down.

Danger closing in would make this a tense picture. But David describes lying down in green pastures beside quiet waters, which points to rest and peace (Psalm 23:2). Keep your eye on the details of this particular scene, baker.

Restores is the word David uses for the LORD's care for his soul (Psalm 23:3). To restore is to renew or bring back to a sound condition. Friend, that reaches deeper than a chance to put your feet up.
Testing would mean putting something to the proof. David's word here is restores, describing the LORD renewing his soul (Psalm 23:3). Think renewal rather than examination, baker.

Weighing measures something, but restoring renews it. David says the LORD restores his soul, not that He weighs it in this verse (Psalm 23:3). I keep the weighing for cookie dough, and somehow still give one cookie the size of a hat.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: David gives that very reason for the LORD's guidance: for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). The His points to the LORD, who is doing the guiding. Notice that David names both the righteous paths and the reason for leading him along them.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: Flock fits the shepherd picture, so I see the connection, baker. But David gives a specific reason here: the LORD guides him in righteous paths for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). A word can fit the picture without being the reason the verse gives.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: We've heard about pastures, but land isn't the reason David gives for this guidance. He says the LORD guides him in paths of righteousness for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). Keep the place in the picture separate from the reason in the sentence.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: David gives the reason plainly: the LORD is with him even in the valley of the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4). He doesn't deny the valley or the evil he might fear. His confidence rests in not facing it alone.

David doesn't point to his own strength here. He says he will fear no evil because the LORD is with him (Psalm 23:4). Friend, the comfort in this line is presence, not having to be strong enough by yourself.
The verse doesn't tell us how long the valley is. David's reason for fearing no evil is that the LORD is with him (Psalm 23:4). His confidence isn't tied to knowing how soon the walk will end.

David names the LORD's rod and staff as a comfort to him (Psalm 23:4). That comfort belongs in the same verse as the valley of the shadow of death. Friend, the difficult setting hasn't erased the reassurance of the shepherd's presence.

David actually says the LORD's rod and staff comfort him (Psalm 23:4). He mentions them after saying the LORD is with him in the valley. In this picture, they bring reassurance rather than another reason to fear.

A table is what the LORD prepares before David (Psalm 23:5). The verse also describes anointed hair and an overflowing cup, building this picture of welcome and provision (Psalm 23:5). Baker, notice how much care David gathers into one scene.

A tent would give us a picture of shelter. Here, David says the LORD prepares a table before him (Psalm 23:5). Stay with that table, because his overflowing cup belongs to this same scene (Psalm 23:5).

A bed might bring rest to mind, friend. But the object the LORD prepares in this verse is a table (Psalm 23:5). David has moved from lying in green pastures to describing a prepared table and an overflowing cup (Psalm 23:2, 5).

David says the table is prepared in the presence of his enemies, not far away from them (Psalm 23:5). The enemies are still part of the scene he describes. The striking detail is that the LORD's provision is there in their presence.

The table isn't described as being somewhere distant from David's enemies. He says the LORD prepares it before him in their presence (Psalm 23:5). Friend, the verse puts that provision and those enemies in the same scene.

An overflowing cup pictures abundance, more than merely having enough (Psalm 23:5). David describes provision that reaches beyond the cup's capacity. I understand capacity until I try to fit one more cookie in a box that has clearly finished accepting applications.

An accidental spill might suggest carelessness in an everyday scene. But David's overflowing cup belongs with the prepared table and anointing, making this a picture of abundant provision (Psalm 23:5). The point is how much he receives, not how carefully he handles a cup.

Overflowing doesn't signal hurry in this picture. Alongside the table and the anointing, David's cup expresses more than enough provision (Psalm 23:5). There is no rushing described in the verse, baker.

David names goodness and mercy as what will follow him throughout his life (Psalm 23:6). He stretches that confidence across all his days, not just the easy ones. Friend, notice the reach of that word all.

Wealth and honor would make this a claim about possessions and standing. David instead names goodness and mercy as what will follow him all his days (Psalm 23:6). Keep his actual pair together, baker, rather than swapping in a different kind of abundance.

Strength and wisdom aren't the two things David names in this closing verse. His words point to goodness and mercy following him throughout his life (Psalm 23:6). It's a particular pair, friend, not a general list of desirable things.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David closes by saying he will dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Psalm 23:6). His final line looks beyond passing relief to a lasting dwelling. I love how the song ends with that settled confidence.

David doesn't name Hebron as his dwelling in this closing line. He says he will dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Psalm 23:6). Friend, the ending points to whose house it is, not to a city on a map.

Canaan isn't the place David names at the end of this psalm. He finishes with the house of the LORD as his dwelling forever (Psalm 23:6). Keep both parts of his ending in view, baker: where he will dwell and how lasting that dwelling is.
